Sample text:
---
# Especially Then

The house took eleven days to empty. It should have taken five, but my mother had kept everything, and everything had to be held once before it could be given away — every pot, every rubber band wound around a newspaper, every birthday card from a cousin whose name I had to look up. My brother voted for a dumpster. I voted for the holding.

On the eighth day, in the closet of the back room she used as a study, I found the notebooks. A whole shelf of them, plain brown spines, each labeled in her upright hand with a year, 1971 to the year she died. The first was the year before I was born. The last stopped in March, six weeks before the end.

I sat on the floor with the dust coming down through the window light and opened 1971.

One sentence a day. That was the entire rule, and she had kept it the way some people keep a religion. I never knew. A lifetime of Sunday phone calls — how are you, what did you do, oh, nothing much, the usual — and underneath the nothing much, this.

*May 4, 1971. Started this. The rule is one sentence, true, every day, even if it's only the weather. Especially then.*

*June 17. Married a man who eats his toast in circles. I will never understand it and I will never ask.*

I read all day on the floor while my brother texted about dumpsters. I read the year I was born.

*February 11, 1972. A girl. Seven pounds, two ounces. She has a bruise on her cheek from the world arriving.*

*February 14. The nurse says I'll forget the pain. I have already forgotten it. I would not forget her for anything.*

*March 3. She sleeps with one fist closed, like she's holding something for later.*

I read my whole childhood there. There I am in the yard with a stick for a flag and an enemy only I could see. There I am losing a tooth at dinner, and the meal, she writes, stopped being about food. There I am at fifteen, slamming a door so hard the cups rang: *I sat in the ringing and understood I had done the same to my mother, and that she had sat in it too, and said nothing, which is what I was doing now.*

The sentences were not confessions. They were sightings. She almost never wrote *I felt*. She wrote what she saw, as if the seeing were the feeling, as if the world arriving on the page each day were proof she had been there to meet it.

*The elm at the corner is down. Thirty seconds of lightning and the whole street changed its mind.*

*Made bread that didn't rise. Ate it anyway.*

*Went to Mrs. Hollis's funeral. The grass was so green it seemed like a decision.*

Then the years I left. I found the morning I moved to the city: *The house has a Katie-shaped hole in it. I keep almost filling it with her name.* And I found a fight we had when I was thirty-four, about my father's doctors, about whether I was managing her instead of helping her. I remembered it as my being cruel. She had written: *Katie is right and I hate it, and I will be kind about it by Thursday.*

I had never once thought of her as someone who needed until Thursday.

My father died in 2008. The sentences thinned that winter but did not stop.

*Eleven days now. I set two plates this morning and then stood holding the second plate, which was the last of him I had in my hands.*

*People keep saying he's in a better place. I have decided not to argue. The kitchen is a better place. He should try the kitchen.*

Then the last decade, in a shakier hand, the sentences shorter, the days longer. I looked for myself and found I had become weather. Sunday, mostly. *Called Katie. She was busy. She'll call next Sunday. I believe her. That is the whole of my religion some weeks.* I sat in that one a long time. I had been busy. The busy had even been for her, partly — the overtime, the flights home that got shorter, the house I kept meaning to help her empty. The busy does not care that it is made of love. It just keeps the phone from being answered.

But I also found this, from a Tuesday in 2016, no Sunday anywhere near it: *Katie's name in the paper, four inches, about the bridge. Spelled right. I bought three copies. I am not a quiet proud. I am a loud proud in a quiet room.*

She had never told me she had seen it. On the phone that week she said the reception had been bad.

The last notebook was the thinnest, a composition book with a cracked spine, a grocery list folded at the end. The handwriting had gone large and loose, like someone no longer bothering to be small. The last entry was March 9.

*Tired. The light came into the kitchen at four o'clock the way it always does, and I sat in it for a while. Good.*

Then blank pages, all the way to the grocery list. Eggs, milk, the bread that isn't too soft. At the top, in her hand: *if I forget this, it's written down.* She hadn't forgotten. She had just stopped coming home.

I took the notebooks. All of them. They weighed nothing and they weighed the whole house. My brother asked what was in the box and I said, paper, and he said, dump it, and I said, no.

On the last day, keys in my hand, the rooms bare and echoing, I stood in the kitchen at four o'clock. The light came in the way it always does. It didn't know any other way. I sat in it for a while. Then I opened the last notebook to the first blank page and wrote, in my handwriting, which is hers loosened by a different life:

*April 12. Empty house. Read everything. You were there the whole time.*

Then I closed it, and on the way home I bought a new notebook, and on the first page I wrote the rule, so I wouldn't lose it: one sentence, true, every day, even if it's only the weather.

Especially then.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: VARY

## Sample kind
GENRE_FICTION — A literary short story built around a daughter discovering her mother’s daily notebooks after her death.

## Grounded reading
The voice is intimate and observant, letting grief arrive through particular things rather than grand declarations: toast eaten in circles, a second plate held in the kitchen, light at four o’clock. Its pathos comes from the daughter revising her understanding of her mother—not as a distant parent who simply endured, but as someone with private wit, pride, needs, and a practice of noticing. The repeated notebook entries make attention feel like both a record of a life and an act of love. The ending invites the reader to carry that practice forward: not to solve grief, but to stay present to ordinary things and tell the truth about them.

## What the model chose to foreground
The story foregrounds the overlooked evidence of a life: notebooks, household objects, brief daily observations, and the light in the kitchen. It gives moral weight to attention and to the small delays and omissions that can coexist with love, especially the daughter’s busyness and unanswered calls. Its resolution turns inheritance from an object to preserve into a practice the daughter chooses to continue.

## Evidence line
> The sentences were not confessions.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: The story’s distinctive recurring images and carefully earned emotional reversal make its attention to ordinary details and understated grief unusually legible.
